claims.text: In the inner disks of nearby massive star-forming spiral galaxies, the kiloparsec-scale star formation rate surface density scales approximately linearly with the molecular gas surface density, corresponding to a roughly constant molecular gas depletion time.

The atomic hydrogen surface density in galactic disks saturates near about 9 solar masses per square parsec, above which the interstellar medium becomes molecular-dominated and below which the star formation rate per unit atomic gas declines strongly toward extended outer disks and dwarf environments.

Across the local galaxy population, both atomic and molecular gas fractions are anti-correlated with total stellar mass, with lower-mass galaxies being systematically more gas-rich than more massive galaxies.

The global molecular gas depletion time varies systematically with a galaxy's specific star formation rate and its offset from the star-forming main sequence, rather than being a single universal constant.

Molecular gas fractions of main-sequence galaxies increase with redshift out to cosmic noon, and this evolution in gas content is closely associated with the rise and subsequent decline of the cosmic star formation rate density.

The global star formation rate correlates tightly and nearly linearly with the mass of dense molecular gas traced by HCN emission, across systems ranging from normal galaxies to ultra-luminous infrared galaxies.
When averaged over whole galaxies, the total atomic-plus-molecular gas surface density and the star formation rate surface density follow a super-linear power law with an index near 1.4.

The cosmic volume-averaged density of molecular hydrogen peaks around redshift 1.5 to 3 and declines by roughly a factor of six to the present day, while the cosmic atomic hydrogen density remains comparatively flat over the same epochs.

Gas-regulator and equilibrium models that integrate the observed cosmic densities of stellar mass, star formation rate, and atomic and molecular gas indicate that continuous large-scale gas accretion is required to sustain star formation in main-sequence galaxies over cosmic time.

Long-wavelength Rayleigh-Jeans dust continuum emission, calibrated against local galaxies with resolved gas and dust mapping, serves as an empirical proxy for the total interstellar medium gas mass in massive, near-solar-metallicity high-redshift galaxies.

Whether the star-formation law is intrinsically super-linear with total gas surface density or strictly linear once the molecular phase is isolated is debated, with the global super-linear slope potentially reflecting averaging over the atomic-to-molecular phase transition.
claims.debate_topic: Linear vs super-linear molecular Kennicutt-Schmidt slope

claims.text: It remains debated whether disk and starburst galaxies occupy two physically distinct sequences of gas depletion time or instead follow a single continuous relation that varies smoothly with offset from the main sequence, a tension linked to assumptions about the CO-to-H2 conversion factor.
claims.debate_topic: Bimodal starburst sequence vs continuous main-sequence scaling

claims.text: The magnitude and physical drivers of systematic variations in the CO-to-H2 conversion factor are contested, with some approaches applying near-uniform values while resolved dust and dynamical calibrations find continuous variation with metallicity, gas surface density, and velocity dispersion.
claims.debate_topic: Magnitude and drivers of CO-to-H2 conversion factor variation

claims.text: Whether galaxy quenching is driven primarily by exhaustion or removal of cold gas or by kinematic and morphological suppression of star formation efficiency in retained gas reservoirs remains an open question, with different galaxy samples supporting different interpretations.
claims.debate_topic: Gas starvation vs kinematic/morphological SFE suppression in quenching

claims.text: After controlling for main-sequence offset, it is debated whether the molecular gas depletion time is constant across cosmic time or shows a mild decline toward higher redshift, a tension attributed to cross-calibration systematics between star formation and molecular gas tracers.
claims.debate_topic: Constant vs mildly evolving depletion time at fixed main-sequence offset

claims.text: Whether elevated star formation in starbursts is driven mainly by a higher fraction of dense gas at fixed dense-gas efficiency or by an intrinsic increase in the star formation efficiency of the dense gas itself is unresolved, partly because of optical-depth and excitation effects in dense-gas tracers.
claims.debate_topic: Dense gas fraction vs dense gas star-formation efficiency as the driver of starbursts

claims.text: Blind molecular line surveys agree on the broad shape of the cosmic molecular gas density history but differ on its peak amplitude and precise peak redshift, a discrepancy attributed to cosmic variance in narrow deep fields and to CO excitation-ladder conversion assumptions.
claims.debate_topic: Magnitude and peak redshift of the cosmic H2 density history
